turns.prompt_text: I struggle to understand how much computer memory I have to use. I have 16 GB of ram on both my Macs, yet I don’t understand how much I have available whenever I look at activity monitor or top or htop.
turns.response_html:
macOS treats unused RAM as wasted RAM. Instead of leaving memory empty, the operating system dynamically fills free space with file caches to keep apps snappy.

Because of this, traditional "Free RAM" is almost always close to zero on a Mac, which makes standard tools like top or htop misleading.

What to Look At in Activity Monitor

To see your actual memory health, open Activity Monitor $\rightarrow$ Memory tab and look at the bottom panel:

  • Memory Pressure (The Real Metric):
    • Green: You have plenty of headroom. macOS is managing caching efficiently, and you don't need to close anything.
    • Yellow: Memory is tightening. macOS is actively compressing memory. Performance may soon dip.
    • Red: You have fully exhausted your 16 GB. macOS is aggressively swapping to your SSD.
  • App Memory: RAM actively held by open software and running processes.
  • Wired Memory: Critical system data that cannot be compressed or moved to the SSD.
  • Compressed: Inactive app memory that macOS compressed to save space instead of writing it out to disk.
  • Cached Files: Data kept in RAM "just in case" to speed up reads. This is your true available pool. The second an app needs memory, macOS immediately drops these caches and hands the RAM over.
  • Swap Used: Data pushed out of RAM and written to your SSD. A few megabytes or low gigabytes is fine, but continuous high swap paired with red memory pressure causes noticeable slowdowns.

Why top and htop Confuse the Picture

Command-line utilities ported from Linux or older Unix architectures often classify cached files as "used."

  • htop will frequently show 14–15 GB used out of 16 GB simply because macOS cached recent disk activity.
  • In macOS's built-in top, look at the PhysMem line: unused is purely empty memory, while the real headroom is roughly unused + purgeable + inactive file-backed cache.

As a rule of thumb: Usable Memory $\approx$ Free + Cached Files, and as long as the Memory Pressure graph is Green, your 16 GB is handling the workload with capacity to spare.

turns.prompt_text: It would be nice to be able to understand the memory weight of different programs. I guess more in terms of what I'm using them for because Google Chrome is pretty heavy but it seems to increase over time through memory leaks. Same with some other applications
turns.response_html:
Different applications consume memory in fundamentally different ways based on their architecture and workload.

Application CategoryTypical Base RAMHeavy / Long-Uptime RAMWhy It Balloons Over Time
Web Browsers (Chrome, Arc, Brave)1.5 – 3 GB6 – 10+ GBIndividual multi-process tabs, complex JavaScript SPAs, extension leaks, and media caching.
Electron / Web-Wrapper Apps (Slack, Discord, VS Code, Notion)500 MB – 1 GB (per app)2 – 4 GBEach app runs its own bundled Chromium instance and Node runtime; cached DOM states build up.
Native Productivity & Note Apps (Obsidian, Pages, Notes)150 – 400 MB500 MB – 1.5 GBMinimal footprint, though large graph views or plugin ecosystems can slowly increase heap size.
Compilers & Build Toolchains (Rust/rustc, Clang, Webpack)200 MB (idle)4 – 12 GB (compiling)Heavy peak usage during link-time optimization (LTO) and macro expansion; drops back down immediately upon completion.
Creative / CAD / Audio (Blender, OpenSCAD, DAWs)1 – 2 GB4 – 8+ GBMesh geometry in RAM, undos/history stacks, and live audio sample buffers.
System Utilities & Daemons (Docker, Window managers)50 – 200 MB1 – 4+ GBDocker allocates a static Linux VM slice; daemons with unbounded event logging slowly leak.

Why Applications Swell Over Time

  • JavaScript Heap & DOM Leaks: Modern web apps and Electron wrappers constantly generate and discard DOM elements. When event listeners or detached DOM nodes aren't dereferenced, the JavaScript garbage collector cannot free them, causing linear memory growth until restarted.
  • V8 JIT Cache Accumulation: Engines like V8 (in Chrome and Electron) compile hot JavaScript code into machine code on the fly. These compiled blocks and inline caches persist in memory for the life of the process.
  • Process Sprawl: Browsers assign separate operating system processes to every tab, extension, renderer, and audio stream to prevent crashes. While secure and stable, each process incurs its own runtime overhead.
  • Undo History & File Buffers: Apps that maintain extensive undo stacks (code editors, 3D modeling tools, graphics suites) keep historical object graphs in active memory unless explicitly cleared.

How to Inspect Specific App Weight

  • Chrome Built-in Task Manager: Press Shift + Esc inside Chrome (or go to Window $\rightarrow$ Task Manager). This breaks down exact memory per tab, extension, and background worker, pinpointing which single webpage is holding 1.5 GB.
  • Activity Monitor "Real Memory" Column: In Activity Monitor, right-click the table header and enable Real Memory alongside Memory. "Memory" reflects virtual allocations, while "Real Memory" shows physical RAM occupied.
  • CLI Memory Inspection: Run top -o mem to sort live processes by physical footprint, or target a specific suspected process with vmmap -summary <PID> in the Terminal to see heap vs. framework allocations.
